early.q: Which of these is where tannin actually comes from?
opts: The color of the grape juice
early.fact: Tannin is extracted from skins, seeds, stems, and oak barrels — not created by fermentation itself.

late.q: Which winemaking choice increases tannin extraction the most?
late.fact: Extended maceration keeps skins in contact with the juice longer, pulling more tannin into the wine.

early.q: Which grape is known for high tannin?
early.fact: Nebbiolo (Barolo, Barbaresco) is famous for high tannin alongside high acidity.

late.q: Which of these reds is typically higher in tannin?
late.fact: Cabernet Sauvignon's thick skins give it more tannin than thin-skinned Pinot Noir or Gamay.

early.q: What does tannin feel like in your mouth?
opts: A drying, gripping feeling on your gums and tongue
A tingling fizz on the tongue
A warming burn in the throat
early.fact: Tannin binds to proteins in your saliva, which is why it feels drying.

late.q: Why does red wine usually have more tannin than white wine?
opts: Red wine ferments with the grape skins; white juice is usually pressed off them first
Red wine always ages longer in bottle
Tannin is added to red wine by law
late.fact: Skin contact during fermentation is where most tannin is extracted.

early.q: Besides the grapes, where else can a wine pick up tannin?
early.fact: New oak barrels release their own wood tannins into the wine.

late.q: How does tannin usually change as a red wine ages in bottle?
late.fact: Over time tannins bind together and can drop out as sediment, so the wine feels softer.

early.q: Which food makes a very tannic red feel smoother?
early.fact: Protein and fat bind with tannin, so rich meat softens a grippy red.

late.q: Thin-skinned grapes tend to make wines with…
late.fact: Tannin comes largely from skins, so thin-skinned grapes like Pinot Noir give lighter tannins.

early.q: Which of these wines usually has the least tannin?
early.fact: White wines spend little time on their skins, so they have very little tannin.

late.q: What is the sediment sometimes found in old red wine bottles?
opts: Tannins and colour pigments that have bonded and settled out
A sign the wine has gone bad
late.fact: As red wine ages, tannins and pigments link up and settle. It's harmless, and why old reds are often decanted.

early.q: What does high acidity in wine actually do?
opts: Makes your mouth water and cuts through fat
early.fact: Acidity is what makes wine food-friendly — it cuts through richness and cleanses the palate.

late.q: Why should tannic red wine generally be avoided with fish?
opts: Tannin reacts with fish oils to taste metallic
Fish is too acidic for red wine
There's no real reason, it's just tradition
late.fact: Tannin binds with the oils in fish, creating an unpleasant metallic taste.

early.q: Which of these wines is typically highest in acidity?
early.fact: Riesling is prized for vivid, energetic acidity across nearly every style it's made in.

late.q: Which pairing follows "acid loves acid"?
opts: A crisp Sauvignon Blanc with a lemony vinaigrette salad
A soft, low-acid red with the same salad
A sweet dessert wine with the same salad
Acidity in wine doesn't interact with food acidity
late.fact: Matching or exceeding a dish's acidity keeps the wine from tasting flat next to it.

early.q: How can you tell a wine is high in acidity when you taste it?
opts: It feels hot in your throat
early.fact: Acidity triggers saliva, so that mouth-watering feeling is the tell.

late.q: Why does a sweet dessert wine need good acidity?
opts: To stop it tasting cloying or flabby
Acidity has no effect on sweet wine
late.fact: Acidity balances sugar, which is why great Sauternes and Tokaji still taste fresh.

early.q: Grapes grown in cooler climates usually give wines with…
early.fact: Cool weather slows ripening, so grapes keep more of their natural acidity.

late.q: Why does high-acid sparkling wine pair so well with fried food?
opts: The acidity and bubbles cut through the oil and refresh your palate
Fried food makes the wine taste sweeter
late.fact: Acidity scrubs fat from the palate, so each bite and sip feels fresh.

early.q: Which dish suits a crisp, high-acid white best?
opts: Goat's cheese salad with a vinaigrette
early.fact: Tangy goat's cheese and vinaigrette need an equally zesty wine; Sancerre with goat's cheese is the classic example.

late.q: What happens when a wine is less acidic than the food it's served with?
opts: The wine tastes flat and dull
The wine tastes sweeter and richer
late.fact: Acidic food makes a softer wine seem flabby, so the wine should match or beat the dish's acidity.

early.q: Which of these is known as a high-acid red grape?
early.fact: Sangiovese's bright acidity is a big part of why Chianti is so food-friendly.

late.q: Why is a high-acid Italian red a good match for tomato-based pasta?
opts: Its acidity matches the acidity of the tomatoes
Italian reds are always low in alcohol
Any wine works equally well with tomato
late.fact: Tomatoes are acidic, so high-acid reds like Chianti or Barbera keep their freshness alongside them.

early.q: On a European wine label, what does the region name usually tell you?
opts: The grape variety, because it's implied by law
The exact vintage style every year
early.fact: A Chablis is legally Chardonnay, a Barolo is legally Nebbiolo — the region implies the grape.

late.q: Which is more specific: a single named vineyard or a broad regional appellation?
opts: Neither is more specific than the other
late.fact: Appellation systems nest from broad region down to village, then single vineyard — each step narrower.

early.q: Which of these is a wine region, not a grape?
early.fact: Chablis is a place in Burgundy; the grape grown there is Chardonnay.

late.q: Rioja wines are legally required to be made mostly from which grape?
late.fact: Tempranillo is Rioja's backbone grape, though blends can include others.

early.q: Sancerre is a place in the Loire. Which grape makes white Sancerre?
early.fact: White Sancerre is Sauvignon Blanc; the label names the place, not the grape.

late.q: In Burgundy, which level sits at the top of the vineyard hierarchy?
late.fact: Burgundy climbs from regional, to village, to Premier Cru, to Grand Cru.

early.q: What does AOC (or AOP) on a French label tell you?
opts: The wine comes from a legally defined area and follows its rules
The wine was aged in oak
early.fact: Appellation rules set where the grapes grow and often which grapes and methods are allowed.

late.q: Which Italian classification sits just below DOCG?
late.fact: Italy's ladder runs from table wine, to IGT, to DOC, with DOCG at the top.

early.q: Why do many New World labels name the grape rather than the region?
opts: Their regions don't legally dictate which grapes are grown
European law forbids naming the region
Grape names are cheaper to print
early.fact: With no laws tying grapes to places, producers lead with the variety: Napa Cabernet, Marlborough Sauvignon Blanc.

late.q: Barolo and Barbaresco are both made from which grape?
late.fact: Both Piedmont appellations require 100% Nebbiolo.

early.q: Where can a sparkling wine legally called Champagne come from?
opts: Only the Champagne region of France
Anywhere, if it's made by the traditional method
early.fact: Champagne is a protected name; similar wines from elsewhere are called Crémant, Cava and so on.

late.q: What does 'Classico' mean in Chianti Classico?
opts: The original, historic heart of the Chianti zone
Any Chianti over ten years old
A Chianti made only from Merlot
late.fact: Classico marks the historic core zone between Florence and Siena.

early.q: What does oak ageing typically add to a wine?
opts: More sweetness from sugar in the wood
early.fact: Oak contributes flavour compounds like vanillin and lactones — not sugar or alcohol.

late.q: Which oak type leans toward coconut and dill rather than vanilla and baking spice?
late.fact: American oak's chemistry leans coconut and dill; French oak leans vanilla and baking spice.

early.q: Which wine style is most likely to show noticeable oak?
early.fact: Classic buttery Chardonnay gets that character from oak ageing plus malolactic fermentation.

late.q: A wine aged in stainless steel instead of oak will typically taste:
late.fact: Steel is neutral and airtight — it preserves fruit character without adding flavour.

early.q: Which flavour is a common sign of new oak?
early.fact: New oak releases vanillin, the same compound that gives vanilla its flavour.

late.q: Why do coopers 'toast' the inside of oak barrels?
opts: Heating the wood creates toasty, smoky, spicy flavours
late.fact: Light, medium or heavy toast changes how much toast, spice and smoke a barrel gives the wine.

early.q: Why does a new oak barrel flavour wine more than an old one?
opts: Each use draws more of the wood's flavour out
Old barrels are made from different trees
Old barrels are lined with steel
early.fact: A barrel's flavour fades with every fill; after a few uses it's close to neutral.

late.q: Besides flavour, what does barrel ageing let into the wine?
late.fact: Wood is slightly porous, and slow oxygen exposure softens tannins and builds complexity.

early.q: Which of these wines is typically aged in oak?
early.fact: Rioja's rules require time in oak for Crianza, Reserva and Gran Reserva.

late.q: How can a winemaker add oak flavour without using barrels?
opts: Adding oak chips or staves to the tank
late.fact: Chips and staves are a cheaper way to give oak character to wines at lower prices.

early.q: A wine described as 'unoaked' has…
opts: Been made without oak, so it tastes of fruit rather than wood
Been aged in extra new oak
early.fact: Unoaked wines, often made in stainless steel, keep a purer, crisper fruit character.

late.q: Which grape is famously made both oaked and unoaked, with very different results?
late.fact: Chablis is often unoaked and steely, while many Californian Chardonnays are rich and oaky.

early.q: What does the vintage year on a label actually represent?
opts: The year the grapes were picked
The year the wine was bottled
The year the wine will taste best
A quality grade the wine earns
early.fact: Vintage simply records the harvest year — a weather report, not a fixed grade.

late.q: In which kind of climate does vintage variation matter most?
opts: Cool, marginal climates like Burgundy or Mosel
Warm, reliable climates like much of California
late.fact: Marginal climates swing more between a great year and a difficult one.

early.q: What does "NV" mean on a Champagne label?
opts: Non-vintage — a blend of multiple years
early.fact: NV wines blend several years deliberately, to keep a consistent house style.

late.q: An older vintage of the same wine, all else equal, is generally:
late.fact: Age moves a wine along its development curve — not automatically up or down in quality.

early.q: Why can the same wine taste different from one year to the next?
opts: Each year's weather affects the grapes
The recipe changes by law every year
It can't; every year tastes identical
early.fact: Sun, rain, frost and heat shape how ripe the grapes get, so each vintage has its own character.

late.q: What does a very hot growing season often lead to?
opts: Riper grapes, bolder fruit and higher alcohol
late.fact: Heat raises sugar in the grapes, and fermentation turns that sugar into alcohol.

early.q: Which of these is a vintage wine?
opts: Any wine over ten years old
Any wine sold in a gift box
early.fact: A vintage wine's grapes come from the harvest year on the label.

late.q: What is a common problem in a cold, rainy vintage?
opts: Rot and diluted flavour in the grapes
late.fact: Rain near harvest swells the grapes and encourages rot, which thins out flavour.

early.q: What do vintage charts rate?
opts: How good the growing season was in each region and year
Only the size of the harvest
early.fact: Vintage charts are a rough guide to weather-driven quality, region by region.

late.q: Why does vintage matter less for many big-brand wines?
opts: Producers blend to keep a consistent house style
Vintage isn't allowed on their labels
They're only made in years with perfect weather
late.fact: Large producers blend across many vineyards so each release tastes much like the last.

early.q: What can a hard frost in spring do to a vineyard?
opts: Kill the new buds and shrink the harvest
early.fact: Spring frost can destroy young shoots, sometimes wiping out much of that year's crop.

late.q: Why are Bordeaux vintages watched so closely?
opts: Its maritime climate makes quality swing from year to year
Bordeaux only releases wine every other year
Its weather is identical every year
Vintage isn't printed on Bordeaux labels
late.fact: Atlantic weather means some Bordeaux years are great and others difficult, which moves prices a lot.

early.q: What does malolactic fermentation (MLF) do?
opts: Converts sharp malic acid into softer lactic acid
early.fact: MLF is a bacterial conversion that softens a wine's acidity and can add a creamy texture.

late.q: Which wine style most reliably signals malolactic fermentation?
late.fact: That buttery, creamy character in Chardonnay is a textbook MLF signature.

early.q: MLF is sometimes called wine's "second fermentation." Is that accurate?
opts: Yes — it's a secondary conversion after alcoholic fermentation
No — it happens before alcoholic fermentation
No — it's the same process as alcoholic fermentation
Yes, and it produces more alcohol
early.fact: MLF is a separate, secondary conversion, usually happening after primary alcoholic fermentation.

late.q: Which wines almost always skip MLF to preserve zesty acidity?
late.fact: Winemakers deliberately block MLF in aromatic, high-acid whites like Riesling to keep that zing.

early.q: Malolactic fermentation is carried out by…
early.fact: Lactic acid bacteria convert malic acid into lactic acid.

late.q: Which by-product of MLF gives some wines a buttery aroma?
late.fact: Diacetyl forms during MLF and is the compound that smells like butter.

early.q: After malolactic fermentation, a wine usually tastes…
early.fact: Lactic acid is gentler than malic acid, so the wine feels smoother.

late.q: Why do most red wines go through malolactic fermentation?
opts: It softens their acidity and makes them more stable
late.fact: Finishing MLF before bottling softens a red and stops it from starting up again in the bottle.

early.q: Malic acid is the sharp acid also found in…
early.fact: Malic acid gives green apples their tartness; MLF swaps it for softer lactic acid.

late.q: Why might a winemaker block MLF in a white wine?
opts: To keep it crisp and fresh
late.fact: Stopping MLF keeps the sharper malic acid, preserving a zesty, fresh style.

early.q: Lactic acid, which MLF produces, is also found in…
early.fact: Lactic acid gives dairy its soft tang, the same softness MLF brings to wine.

late.q: What does MLF do to a wine's overall acidity?
late.fact: Lactic acid is weaker than malic acid, so converting one to the other lowers total acidity.
